How fast does information online have to travel for me to be able to communicate with others around the world instantly?
A 56k modem is fast enough for more text than you could ever read. The entire Library of Congress is just 11 TB if only text is counted, and they have miles of shelving.

If the data is in small packages, like text only, then it already comes pretty close to instant. But no transmission speed can be faster than the speed of light. To get as close to that as possible, you would need to have a direct (high end) fiber optic connection with no other types of non-fiber connections between the transmission points.

Online speed isn't really measured in the sense of what we think of as travel speed. Rather, it is measured more in terms of quantities of data (bits, bytes, etc.) that can be transmitted through various wires, cables, and waves, per second.

Traditional copper wires can only transmit a limited amount of data (aka data speed) because when electricity flows through copper wires it magnetizes the wires which in turn interferes with the electrical data pulses that the wire is carrying. Too many data pulses of electricity = too much magnetism = garbled transmissions. That's why fiber optic (laser data pulses) transmission are so much "faster."

Wireless transmissions are a little different. Their data pulses are limited by wave frequency- how many waves (carrying data bits, pulses) can hit a target per second, and also by atmospheric conditions like humidity, air molecules, walls, etc, physically blocking waves.

That is why the higher frequencies allowed by the 5G protocol will send much, much "faster" data transmissions. 5G will be able to transmit as much data per second as mid range fiber optic cables, and will allow telcoms to bypass copper wires by using the 5G network to connect to other 5G systems, and directly link to fiber optic cables as well.

Sorry for rambling, and I skipped over a lot of points to try to keep it simple.

TL;DR Assuming you are looking for real-time, voice/video chat, what you are looking for (close to it) will soon be a reality with 5G networks.

It depends on how you define "instant" and "communicate". If someone's text-chat reply to you is offset from real-time by 1 second, that could be latency, or it could be they've taken an extra second to consider their reply... the difference isn't really important. But in a video-chat, that same 1 second delay could mean the difference between accidentally talking-over the other person or not... so the medium is important to the question.
